findings.finding: Insights: Scores are binary sums of round points; after each round winners (faster of each pair) gain the round’s power‑2 value. Pairings must match equal scores, so each round halves each score group. The only possible final score distribution is the full binary ranking: each runner ends with a unique score 0…2²⁰‑1, determined solely by the order of wins, which is forced by speed ordering. Thus the final ordering is fixed; N=1, so k=0. (Avoid assuming ties; they never occur.)

Insights: Final scores are binary numbers; each round i decides the i‑th bit (2^{20‑i}) for every runner. Pairings can arbitrarily choose which equal‑score runners compete, so any permutation of the 2^{20} binary strings consistent with speed order is possible. N = (2^{20})! (all orderings). Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N) via Legendre: v_p((2^{20})!) = Σ⌊2^{20}/p^j⌋. k = min(v₂,v₅). Return k mod 100000. Pitfall: Ensure no extra constraints limit permutations; verify all orderings achievable.

Insights: Final scores are unique binary strings of 20 bits; ordering equals sorting by these strings. Any permutation respecting the “binary‑tree” partial order (parent beats children) can occur. Count linear extensions of this poset → N = (2^{20})! / ∏_{v} size(subtree_v). Compute v₂(N), v₅(N); k = min(v₂,v₅). Beware: subtree sizes are powers of 2, so denominator contributes only 2’s, not 5’s. Thus v₅(N)=v₅((2^{20})!) and v₂(N)=v₂((2^{20})!)-∑(log₂ subtree). Finally k = v₅((2^{20})!). Compute k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Final scores are binary strings of length 20; each round splits each equal‑score group into winners/losers. Winners must be a “ballot” subset of half the group (no prefix has more winners than losers). Number of possible winner sets for a group of size 2m is Catalan Cₘ. Thus total orderings = product over rounds of Catalan numbers for groups of size 2^{20‑i+1}. Compute N = ∏_{i=1}^{20} C_{2^{20‑i}}. Find largest k with 10^k|N; output k mod 10⁵. Pitfall: ensure Catalan formula Cₙ = (2n choose n)/(n+1) and count 2‑adic/5‑adic valuations correctly.

Insights: Final scores are distinct binary strings of length 20; ranking = descending binary value. Process builds a perfect binary tree: at each node (size 2^{20‑d}) we split runners into equal halves (winners/losers) via a perfect matching where each winner beats its paired loser. Thus a permutation is realizable iff for every node the faster 2^{19‑d} runners can be matched to the slower 2^{19‑d} ones. This is equivalent to the condition that in each node the set of winners is exactly the faster half of that node’s runners (any ordering of those halves is allowed). Hence the number of possible final orderings equals the product over all internal nodes of ( (size/2)! )², i.e. N = ∏_{i=0}^{19} (2^{20‑i‑1}!)^{2·2^{i}}. Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N) via Legendre’s formula, take k = min(v₂,v₅), then output k mod 100 000. (Key pitfall: ensure each node’s halves are unordered; multiply factorials accordingly.)

Insights: After each round each score‑group of size 2^{m} splits evenly into winners/losers, so final scores are all binary numbers 0…2^{20}−1. Winners at a node must all be faster than losers they beat, i.e. a perfect matching exists iff the k fastest of the node are not all placed in the loser side. Thus any partition of a node into two equal halves is feasible iff the faster half (by speed) can be chosen as winners. Consequently the tournament can realize any total order that respects the recursive “top‑half before bottom‑half” hierarchy of a perfect binary tree. Counting such linear extensions yields N; find the exponent of 10 in N and output k mod 10⁵. (Key pitfall: assuming any partition works; must enforce Hall’s condition.)

Insights: After each round each score pattern appears equally often; after 20 rounds scores are a permutation of 0…2²⁰‑1, so no ties. N = #permutations realizable by pairing rules. Model as binary tournament: at round i participants with same (i‑1)-bit prefix are paired; faster wins gets bit 1. Count assignments of speeds to final binary ranks respecting that in every internal node the winner must be faster than loser. This equals number of linear extensions of the poset defined by the complete binary tree where each node orders its two children (winner > loser). Compute N = product over all internal nodes of (size of subtree left + size right choose size left) = ∏_{k=0}^{19} (2^{k+1} choose 2^{k})^{2^{20‑k‑1}}. Then k = v₁₀(N); find k mod 10⁵. (Pitfall: ensure exponent counts correctly; avoid assuming all permutations possible.)

Insights: Final scores are distinct 20‑bit strings; ranking = descending binary order. Pairings each round give constraints: for every match, winner’s bit = 1 must precede loser’s bit = 0 in final order. Thus the set of possible rankings equals the number of linear extensions of the poset defined by 20 rounds of perfect‑matching comparisons (each vertex compared once per round). Compute N = #extensions for 2²⁰‑vertex graph formed by 20 successive perfect matchings; then find largest k with 10ᵏ|N and output k mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: assuming all permutations possible (false); need exact count via recursive formula or DP on tree‑like structure of matchings. Use symmetry: each round halves groups → poset is a complete binary tree where each internal node imposes “winner before loser”. Number of extensions = product over nodes of binomial(L+R, L) where L,R are sizes of sub‑posets; for full tree of depth 20 this equals ∏_{i=0}^{19} (2^{i+1} choose 2^{i})^{2^{19-i}}. Compute exponent of 2 and 5 in N, get k = min(v₂(N),v₅(N)). Finally output k mod 100000.

Insights: Winners/losers in any equal‑score group of size 2k are exactly the “ballot” subsets → Catalan Cₖ possibilities. Choices at different groups are independent and give a unique final ranking.  

Thus  

\[
N=\prod_{k=1}^{20}C_{2^{k-1}}^{\,2^{20-k}},\qquad 
C_m=\frac1{m+1}\binom{2m}{m}.
\]

Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N); k=min(v₂,v₅). Use Legendre’s formula for factorial valuations in Cₘ. Finally output k mod 10⁵. (Beware overflow – work modulo 10⁵ for the final answer.)

Insights: Final scores are distinct binary strings of length 20, so rankings = all possible leaf‑labelings of a full binary tree. Number of rankings  

\(N=\prod_{m=2}^{20}C_{2^{m-1}}^{\,2^{20-m}}\)  

with Catalan \(C_n=\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1)\).

Compute 5‑adic valuation:  

\(v_5(C_n)=\frac{2s_5(n)-s_5(2n)}4-v_5(n+1)\) ( \(s_5\) = sum of base‑5 digits).  

Set \(n=2^{t}\) for \(t=1\ldots19\).  

Then  

\(v_5(N)=\sum_{t=1}^{19}2^{19-t}\,v_5(C_{2^{t}})\).

Use the formula above (or program) to get \(v_5(N)={answer = 0}\) → largest \(k\) with \(10^k\mid N\) is \(k=0\); answer \(0\). (Pitfall: Catalan numbers \(C_{2^k}\) are even, not odd.)

Insights: Final scores are distinct 20‑bit numbers. Ranking = ordering of leaves of a binary tree where each node (size 2^m) splits its 2^m players into winners/losers of size 2^{m‑1}. Winners must form a “ballot” (Dyck) subset → Catalan C_{2^{m‑1}} choices. Recurrence: f(0)=1, f(m)=C_{2^{m‑1}}·f(m‑1)^2. Hence N=f(20)=∏_{i=0}^{19}C_{2^i}^{2^{19‑i}}. Compute 5‑adic valuation: v₅(N)=∑_{i=0}^{19}2^{19‑i}[v₅((2·2^i)!)-2v₅((2^i)!)-v₅(2^i+1)] =121 818. v₂(N)=2^{19}‑1>v₅, so k=v₅=121 818. Answer k mod 10⁵ = **21818**. Pitfalls: ensure round points are 2^{20‑i}, use Catalan for ballot subsets, subtract vₚ(n+1) (not factorial).
